Fall Pumpkin Table Runner Pattern: An Easy FPP Project for Fall

I love decorating for fall, but I don’t necessarily want fall decorations everywhere. Part of that is practical. I have a smaller house, and it doesn’t take much before seasonal decorating starts to feel like a little too much.

That’s one reason I like quilted table runners. They add just enough color and texture to make a room feel different for the season. And when fall is over? Fold it up and tuck it away until next year.

My Fall Pumpkin Table Runner was designed with exactly that in mind.

It’s a small, manageable quilting project with three foundation paper pieced pumpkins. The finished runner measures approximately 15″ x 36″, which makes it a nice size for a dining table, coffee table, console, or buffet.

And there’s another reason I especially like this project. If foundation paper piecing has always made you a little nervous, these pumpkins are a good place to try it out.

A Small Fall Quilting Project That Makes a Big Difference

Not every project needs to be a bed-sized quilt.

Sometimes you just want to pull out a few fabrics, sit down at your sewing machine, and make something you can actually finish. That’s the idea behind my Fast Finish Projects.

They’re smaller projects that let you practice a skill, use some of the fabric you already have, and enjoy that wonderful feeling that comes from finishing something.

The Fall Pumpkin Table Runner fits right into that category. The runner is made from three pumpkin blocks with simple sashing and borders. Once the pumpkins are pieced, the rest of the construction will probably feel very familiar.

It’s seasonal without being fussy. And because it’s only 15″ x 36″, you can add a little fall color to your home without having pumpkins taking over every available surface.

(Unless you like pumpkins taking over every available surface. In that case, carry on.)

Don’t Let Foundation Paper Piecing Scare You

I know foundation paper piecing can look intimidating.

There’s paper involved. The fabric seems to be going in the wrong direction. And when you first look at an FPP template, you may wonder why anyone would choose to quilt this way.

But here’s the thing.

Foundation paper piecing is much easier once you understand the process.

You’re sewing your fabric in a specific order using the printed template as your guide. One of the reasons quilters love FPP is the accuracy you can get from the technique.

And these pumpkins don’t require complicated sections with dozens of tiny pieces.

The pumpkin body is foundation paper pieced, the stem section is pieced separately, and then the two sections are joined together. Make three pumpkins, add the sashing and borders, and your table runner top is ready to quilt.

New to Foundation Paper Piecing?

If you’ve never tried FPP before, I recommend working through my How to Foundation Paper Piece tutorial first.

It walks you through the process so you can understand what you’re doing before you begin your pumpkins.

Try it out. Once the process clicks, I think you’ll discover that foundation paper piecing isn’t nearly as mysterious as it first appears.

Why This Pumpkin Table Runner Is a Good First FPP Project

One of the easiest ways to learn a new quilting technique is to use it in a small project.

You get enough repetition to understand what you’re doing, but you’re not committing yourself to making 48 blocks while you figure it out.

With this project, you make just three pumpkin blocks. That gives you three opportunities to practice the same FPP process. By the time you get to that third pumpkin, things should be feeling much more familiar.

After that, you’re back to traditional piecing as you add the sashing and borders.

That combination makes this an approachable project for a confident beginner who already understands the basics of using a sewing machine and making a quilt.

And when you’re finished? You haven’t just practiced foundation paper piecing.

You’ve finished something and every new technique you learn becomes another tool you can use in future quilts.

Pull From Your Stash First

Before you start thinking you need special fall fabric for this project, take a look at what you already have.

You may be surprised by what you find. Obviously, orange works beautifully for pumpkins. But there isn’t just one version of orange.

Look for rust, peach, gold, burnt orange, coral, or even softer shades. And don’t overlook prints. Gingham, dots, stripes, small florals, tone-on-tone fabrics, and other scraps can make wonderful pumpkins.

The table runner can be made bold or minimal simply by changing your fabric choices, and the pattern includes a Project Possibilities page so you can experiment with your ideas before cutting into your fabric.

This is your table runner. Make it look like you.

Make Your Pumpkins Your Own

You don’t even have to stop with the table runner. The pattern also includes a bonus 6″ FPP pumpkin template that works nicely for smaller projects.

Use one pumpkin to make a mug rug. Make several in different fabrics.

Dig through your scrap basket and see what combinations you can come up with. This is where a simple pattern starts becoming your own.

Finishing Your Pumpkin Table Runner

Once the table runner top is finished, you’ll need to quilt and bind it.

Straight-line or diagonal quilting works beautifully on a small project like this. An all-over stipple is another option if you enjoy free-motion quilting.

Choose the quilting that works for you and the tools you already have. Once your quilting is finished, square up the runner and add the binding.

If binding is another one of those steps that makes you hesitate, I have you covered there, too.

My How to Machine Bind a Quilt tutorial will walk you through the process step by step.

You don’t have to know how to do everything before you start. Sometimes you learn the next step when you get there.

What’s Included in the Fall Pumpkin Table Runner Pattern

The Fall Pumpkin Table Runner is a complete PDF pattern designed to take you from fabric selection through your finished project.

Inside you’ll find the following:

  • Instructions and diagrams for making a 15″ x 36″ table runner
  • Fabric requirements and cutting instructions
  • 9″ FPP pumpkin templates
  • Bonus 6″ FPP pumpkin template for smaller projects
  • Project Possibilities page for planning your fabric choices

The pattern also includes plenty of diagrams along the way. I’m a visual learner myself, and sometimes seeing how those pieces fit together makes all the difference.

A Fast Finish for Fall

You don’t need to redecorate your entire house to make it feel like fall. And you don’t need to start another large quilt to spend some meaningful time at your sewing machine.

Sometimes a few pieces of fabric and a small project are enough.

Watch this short video to learn more about the Fall Pumpkin Table Runner.

This little table runner gives you a chance to pull some favorite fabrics from your stash, practice foundation paper piecing, and make something you can actually use when fall rolls around.

And when you put it out again next year, you’ll remember making those pumpkins. That’s part of the quilting journey, too.

If this feels like the kind of project you’d enjoy making this fall, you can take a closer look at the pattern below.
